name: SMAS plication facelift

lead: SMAS plication tightens the layer under the facial skin by folding and stitching it rather than cutting and moving it. It is used for cheeks, jowls and the neck line.
General references describe it as less invasive than deep-plane facelift but with more limited lifting.

paras: Sutured folds in the SMAS pull the deeper facial tissue into a tighter position, and the skin is then redraped.

Facelift risks include hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion. A meta-analysis found sub-SMAS techniques considered to have a higher complication profile than less invasive SMAS techniques. It is surgery.

lead: SMAS plication is a facelift approach in which the superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS), the fibromuscular layer beneath the facial skin, is folded and sutured to tighten it, with little or no extensive dissection of the layer. General references describe it as giving moderate tightening and being less invasive, but with limited mobilization compared with SMAS flap or deep-plane techniques [1].

Variants described in the literature include lateral SMASectomy with plication and short-scar facelifts [2], anterior SMAS plication for prominent nasomandibular folds [3], and platysma-SMAS plication [4]. A study of the face's retaining ligaments also described ligament correction with SMAS plication [5].
Evidence consists mainly of surgeon series and comparative studies, including several comparing plication with deep-plane facelift [6][7].
infobox: SMAS flap or imbrication, deep plane facelift

paras: The SMAS was described in 1976 by Mitz and Peyronie, with the term coined by Paul Tessier [1]. In plication, the surgeon folds the SMAS on itself and secures it with sutures, in contrast to imbrication or flap techniques that cut and reposition the layer. A 1982 study compared plication with imbrication [8]. Lateral SMASectomy removes a portion of SMAS over the anterior parotid and secures the mobile SMAS to the fixed portion, and its describers called it rapid, safe and reproducible [2].

A comparative study in 2004 examined deep-plane facelift against SMAS plication [6], and a 2007 study compared their midface effects [7]. A 2021 study used artificial intelligence and patient satisfaction to compare value of procedure types and specific techniques [9]. A retrospective study of 8,788 facial rejuvenation cases is also reported [10].

A meta-analysis of complication rates among SMAS facelift techniques reported that sub-SMAS techniques are considered to have a higher complication profile, particularly for facial nerve injury, which leads some surgeons to avoid them [11]. General references list hematoma, nerve injury, skin necrosis (higher in smokers), scarring and ear distortion as facelift risks [1].

Human studies include the comparative deep-plane versus plication studies [6][7], the 8,788-case retrospective review [10], and the AI and patient-satisfaction analysis [9]. No randomized trial of SMAS plication specifically was found in the sources reviewed.
